The Threaded sculpin Gymnocanthus pistilliger attains a maximum recorded body length of 28 centimeters [Li = 28 centimeters], a value consistent with the upper size range observed among cottoid fishes inhabiting the continental shelf of the northern Pacific Ocean. Field surveys conducted in the Sea of Okhotsk indicate that adult males generally reach a larger terminal size than females, though the species as a whole rarely exceeds this asymptotic length. Newly emerged prolarvae, which transition from a lecithotrophic to an exotrophic state within days of eclosion, enter the water column at a remarkably small size. Based on the typical egg diameter of approximately 1.63 millimeters for related cottids, the estimated wet weight at birth is 0.0023 grams [Wwb = 0.0023 grams], reflecting the modest endogenous yolk reserves available to the developing embryo before the chorion ruptures and the mouth opens for first prey capture. This neonatal body mass places the species among the smaller-bodied members of the family Cottidae.

Sexual maturation in Threaded sculpin follows a dimorphic pattern that becomes apparent when examining the length-frequency distributions of spawning individuals. Under conditions observed in wild coastal populations, females typically achieve puberty, defined here as the onset of vitellogenesis and ovarian recrudescence, upon reaching a total length of 15.8 centimeters [Lp = 15.8 centimeters]. In contrast, males undergo the corresponding transition to reproductive viability, marked by the commencement of spermatogenesis, at a slightly smaller body size of 14.6 centimeters [Lp = 14.6 centimeters] in total length. These length-based thresholds, which correspond roughly to an age of approximately 2.5 years based on von Bertalanffy growth parameters fitted to field-collected otolith data, imply that both sexes allocate a substantial portion of their early somatic growth to structural development before diverting resources toward gonadal production. The difference between the sexes in maturation length may reflect divergent selective pressures on male and female reproductive strategies within this demersal spawner.

Reproductive output in Gymnocanthus pistilliger has been characterized under controlled laboratory conditions that approximate the thermal regime of its benthic habitat. When maintained at a stable water temperature of 2.9 °C [T = 2.9 °C], gravid females produce a maximum of approximately 12 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 12 eggs per day], a daily fecundity that translates to an estimated annual egg production on the order of several thousand per individual. This maximum reproduction rate is notably high for a sculpin of moderate body size and likely reflects an adaptive response to high larval mortality rates typical of cold-water marine environments where planktonic food resources are seasonally unpredictable. The observed fecundity likely depends on female body condition and the availability of benthic prey during the pre-spawning foraging period. Under the same experimental conditions, females continue to release demersal eggs in adhesive masses over several consecutive days, a pattern consistent with batch spawning.

Longevity data for the Threaded sculpin, derived from mark-recapture studies and validated through annual growth increment analysis of sagittal otoliths, indicate a maximum lifespan of 12 years [am = 12 years] when individuals are reared under a thermal regime averaging 7.6 °C [T = 7.6 °C]. This comparatively extended lifespan, which exceeds that of many smaller-bodied littoral cottids, suggests a life-history strategy favoring delayed senescence and iteroparous reproduction rather than a single, semelparous spawning event. The positive relationship between cooler ambient temperatures and increased lifespan is well documented among ectothermic teleosts and is thought to be mediated by reduced metabolic rates and lower cumulative oxidative damage over time. In the wild, the oldest documented Threaded sculpin specimens have been captured in the deeper, thermally stable waters of the Bering Sea shelf, where seasonal temperature fluctuations are comparatively muted.

The interplay between body size at maturity and reproductive timing shapes the overall demographic structure of Gymnocanthus pistilliger populations. Because females delay first reproduction until reaching a total length of 15.8 centimeters [Lp = 15.8 centimeters], a size that correlates with a minimum age of roughly 2.5 years under average growth conditions, the species exhibits a relatively protracted pre-reproductive period compared to other sculpins in the subarctic North Pacific. This delayed maturation, combined with the moderate fecundity described earlier in relation to the daily egg production rate at 2.9 °C [T = 2.9 °C], may render local populations vulnerable to overexploitation if fishing pressure selectively removes larger, older individuals before they have contributed multiple spawning events. Comparative analyses with the congener Gymnocanthus tricuspis suggest that the Threaded sculpin's life-history syndrome—characterized by moderate size at puberty and a decade-long potential lifespan of 12 years [am = 12 years] at 7.6 °C [T = 7.6 °C]—represents an intermediate position on the fast-slow continuum of teleost life histories.
